description_full: Artesian Resources Corporation provides water, wastewater, and other services in Delaware, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The company distributes and sells water to residential, commercial, industrial, governmental, municipal, and utility customers, as well as for public and private fire protection; and offers wastewater collection, treatment infrastructure, and wastewater services to customers. It also provides contract water and wastewater operations; water, sewer, and internal service line protection plans; and wastewater management services, as well as design, construction, and engineering services. In addition, the company offers services to other water utilities; owns real estate properties, including land for office buildings, a water treatment plant, and wastewater facility; and provides design, installation, maintenance, and repair services. As of December 31, 2025, it served customers in Delaware, Maryland, and Pennsylvania through 1,515 miles of transmission and distribution mains. Artesian Resources Corporation was founded in 1905 and is headquartered in Newark, Delaware.

financial_summary: Artesian Resources Corporation is a small-cap utilities business with a $355M market cap on $113M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $18M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.2×.
Shareholder yield of 3.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.1% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.7) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away

Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sect: Its 25% operating margin is roughly in line with the Utilities median (21%).

mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.42, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $933K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 20% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 29% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $33.00 (margin of safety -4%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 1%).
On multiples it looks cheap against Utilities peers: P/E 15.0 vs 20.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 19% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -5.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.3% (vs the 8% bar).
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 5.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.16).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.77x.
ROE of 9% is amplified by 3.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.2x net debt to EBITDA ($52K of cash against $176.5M of debt), with interest covered 3.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.73 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.64 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.5% over 3 years, 5.1% over 5 years and 3.9% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 3.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 4.3x depreciation (52.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is -12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.1%, and institutions hold 57%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (12 sales, net $771K sold).
It returns 3.5% a year to shareholders (3.7% in dividends).
The share count has grown 2.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 31 consecutive years, raising it 6.2% a year over the last five.
